newsitem.title: USA: World fears for Mideast peace after suicide bombs.
newsitem.headline: World fears for Mideast peace after suicide bombs.

text.p: World leaders reacted in horror to an attack on Wednesday by two Arab suicide bombers in Israel, fearing the 14 deaths and 157 injuries could destroy hopes of Middle East peace.

President Bill Clinton called the bombing in a crowded market in the heart of Jewish West Jerusalem a "barbarous act" and pointedly urged Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority to take action to stop such "terrorist" attacks.

In a hastily-arranged appearance in the White House press room, Clinton said he had telephoned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to express condolences and also said a visit to the Middle East by U.S. mediator Dennis Ross was being postponed to allow a period of mourning in Israel.

"The only answer can and must be concrete steps by the Palestinian Authority to increase security operations and the strengthening of security cooperation between Palestinians and Israelis," Clinton said.
Arafat condemned the bombing and said he would do all he could to confront anti-Israeli militants.

"I condemn completely this terrorist act because it is against the peace process, against the Palestinians, and against the Israelis," Arafat told Reuters. "We will do our (best) to face these terrorist activities as we have done in the past and will do in the future."
Others reacted by calling on Israelis and Palestinians to relaunch negotiations, broken off in March when Israel began building a settlement on the outskirts of Jerusalem.
"This is a crucial time in the quest for peace in the Middle East," said Secretary-General Kofi Annan.
"I appeal to all concerned to reject violence and pursue their aims through dialogue, at the negotiating table," he said in a statement.
Egypt, which became the first Arab state to sign a peace treaty with Israel in 1979, said the Middle East peace process must prevail.
State television said President Hosni Mubarak called Netanyahu to offer his condolences and condemn the attack.
Jordan, which signed its own peace treaty with Israel in 1994, blamed extremists seeking to wreck the Middle East peace process for the deaths.

"Extremists attack any glimmer of hope in pushing the peace process forward whenever the circumstances are created to resume talks or a breakthrough appears on the horizon," a government spokesman told the state news agency Petra.
The Vatican deplored Wednesday's fatal bombing in Jerusalem as an attack against innocent people and said peace in the Middle East could only be achieved through dialogue, not violence.
"It is not with actions of this kind that peace is reached," Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said in a statement.
Norway played a leading role in brokering the secret talks between Israel and the Palestinian Liberation Organisation in 1993, which led to the signing of the historic Oslo peace accords.
Jan Egeland, Norway's Deputy Foreign Minister, told the NTB news agency that the latest bombing had put another stumbling block on the peace trail.
"It will be difficult (to restart talks) to put it mildly," Egeland said.
"Let us be in no doubt. There are powers which want war between Israel and the Palestinians," he said, adding that there were also uncompromising extremist forces in Israel.
These fears were echoed by the European Union, which urged Israelis not to let the attack derail the peace process.

"The European Union presidency calls on the government and people of Israel not to be provoked by those who want to torpedo peace," Luxembourg Foreign Minister Jacques Poos said in a statement on behalf of the 15-nation bloc.
France and Germany, key players in the Middle East peace process, were joined by Britain, South Africa and others in calling for a resumption of peace talks.
But in Syria, a radical exiled group of Palestinians said Netanyahu had only himself to blame for Wednesday's carnage.

"Netanyahu is fully responsible for the escalation of violence and resistance operations because he rejects peace," Maher al-Taher spokesman of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) told Reuters.
